---
title: "Gibbs sampling"
subtitle: "Lecture 4"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can sample a posterior that no single proposal
density can cover, by splitting the parameter vector into blocks and drawing each
block from its own conditional distribution.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For any partition $\theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_B)$ of the parameter vector,
sweeping

$$
\theta_b^{(s)} \;\sim\; \phi\!\left(\theta_b \mid \theta_{-b}^{\text{current}}, y\right),
\qquad b = 1, \dots, B,
$$

leaves the joint posterior $\phi(\theta \mid y)$ invariant, so a chain built from
full conditionals alone has the posterior as its stationary distribution. One
hard sampling problem in $k$ dimensions is thereby replaced by $B$ easy ones, and
the difficulty moves to two new places: every full conditional has to be a
distribution we can draw from, and consecutive draws are dependent, so the
precision of an average is no longer governed by the number of draws.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. diagnose why a fixed proposal density degenerates as the number of parameters
   grows, and quantify the rate;
2. derive the Gibbs sampler from the factorisation of a joint density, and show
   that a block update leaves the posterior invariant;
3. derive the representation of a Student-$t$ variable as a Normal mixed over a
   Gamma scale, and the full conditionals it creates in a linear model with
   arbitrary $n$ and $k$;
4. implement a Gibbs sampler with a latent variable block and a non-standard
   block handled on a grid;
5. diagnose burn-in, autocorrelation and effective sample size from the output of
   one chain;
6. interpret the latent scales as a month-by-month measure of how far outside the
   ordinary each observation was;
7. compare the cost of coordinate-wise updating against the independent sampling
   of the previous chapter.

Week 4 of 15, paired with the [Week 4 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/04-gibbs-sampling.qmd). The chapter assumes the
Monte Carlo estimator, importance weights and the effective sample size of
Lecture 3, and the Normal-inverse-Gamma algebra of Lecture 2.

## Motivation: the proposal that worked on three parameters {#sec-motivation}

The question on the table is the one Lecture 3 opened. A risk desk holding the US
market portfolio wants to know the average monthly excess return it can expect,
how wide an ordinary month is, and how much weight to put on the possibility of a
month far outside the ordinary. The model that answers all three at once gives the
returns a Student-$t$ distribution with unknown location $\mu$, unknown scale
$\sigma$ and unknown degrees of freedom $\nu$, and the answer is the joint
posterior of those three numbers. This chapter does not change the question, the
model or the data; it changes only the machinery that produces the posterior, and
it does so because the machinery of Lecture 3 does not survive contact with the
models that come next.

Lecture 3 left the equity premium problem solved but expensively solved. The
posterior of $\theta = (\mu, \sigma, \nu)$ for monthly market excess returns under
a Student-$t$ likelihood was sampled by importance sampling and by rejection, and
both worked because a proposal with heavy enough tails could be built by hand:
a $t_5$ for the location and for the scale, centred and scaled by a preliminary
look at the posterior, and the prior itself for the degrees of freedom. The
envelope constant that rejection sampling needed was then located numerically over
a grid of nearly four hundred thousand points. Everything in that sentence is
affordable because $\theta$ has three components.

The first chunk rebuilds that proposal on the same $439$ months and scores it, so
that the rest of the chapter argues against a measured number rather than against
a memory.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import time

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from scipy.special import gammaln
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

ff_m = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
sample = ff_m["1990-01":"2026-07"]
r = sample["mkt_rf"].to_numpy()
n = r.size

m_0, s_0 = 0.0, 0.01                      # mu ~ N(m_0, s_0^2)
alpha_0, delta_0 = 3.0, 0.0032            # sigma^2 ~ IG(alpha_0, delta_0)
nu_lo, nu_hi, nu_mean = 2.0, 50.0, 10.0   # nu - 2 ~ Exp(1/nu_mean) truncated to (0, 48]
nu_const = -np.log(nu_mean) - np.log(1.0 - np.exp(-(nu_hi - nu_lo) / nu_mean))

names = ["mu", "sigma", "nu"]
grid_mean = np.array([0.009126, 0.037756, 8.597757])     # Lecture 3, 393,216-point grid
grid_sd = np.array([0.002026, 0.002220, 3.931715])


def log_kernel(mu, sigma, nu):
    """log of the unnormalised posterior, exactly the kernel of Lecture 3."""
    mu, sigma, nu = (np.asarray(a, float).ravel()
                     for a in np.broadcast_arrays(mu, sigma, nu))
    out = np.full(mu.shape, -np.inf)
    ok = (sigma > 0) & (nu > nu_lo) & (nu <= nu_hi)
    m, s, v = mu[ok], sigma[ok], nu[ok]
    z2 = ((r[None, :] - m[:, None]) / s[:, None]) ** 2
    ll = (n * (gammaln((v + 1) / 2) - gammaln(v / 2) - 0.5 * np.log(np.pi * v)
               - np.log(s)) - 0.5 * (v + 1) * np.log1p(z2 / v[:, None]).sum(axis=1))
    lp = (-0.5 * ((m - m_0) / s_0) ** 2
          - (alpha_0 + 1) * np.log(s ** 2) - delta_0 / s ** 2 + np.log(2.0 * s)
          + nu_const - (v - nu_lo) / nu_mean)
    out[ok] = ll + lp
    return out


q_mu = stats.t(df=5, loc=0.00913, scale=0.0022)          # Lecture 3's proposal
q_sig = stats.t(df=5, loc=0.0378, scale=0.0024)
q_nu = stats.truncexpon(b=(nu_hi - nu_lo) / nu_mean, loc=nu_lo, scale=nu_mean)

S_is = 40_000
cand = np.column_stack([q_mu.rvs(S_is, random_state=rng),
                        q_sig.rvs(S_is, random_state=rng),
                        q_nu.rvs(S_is, random_state=rng)])
log_q = (q_mu.logpdf(cand[:, 0]) + q_sig.logpdf(cand[:, 1]) + q_nu.logpdf(cand[:, 2]))
log_w = log_kernel(cand[:, 0], cand[:, 1], cand[:, 2]) - log_q
w_is = np.where(np.isfinite(log_w), np.exp(log_w - np.nanmax(log_w[np.isfinite(log_w)])), 0.0)
w_is /= w_is.sum()
ess_frac = 1.0 / np.sum(w_is ** 2) / S_is

srt = np.sort(w_is)[::-1]
share = np.arange(1, S_is + 1) / S_is
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(np.log10(w_is[w_is > 0] * S_is), bins=80, color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_xlabel(r"$\log_{10}$ of the weight relative to an equal weight")
axes[0].set_ylabel("draws"); axes[0].set_title("Importance weights, three parameters")
axes[1].plot(share, np.cumsum(srt), color="steelblue")
axes[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", label="equal weights")
axes[1].set_xlabel("share of draws, largest weight first")
axes[1].set_ylabel("share of total weight"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_title("How concentrated the weights are")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{n} months, {sample.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {sample.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"effective sample size {1.0 / np.sum(w_is ** 2):,.0f} of {S_is:,} draws "
      f"({ess_frac:.3f} of them)")
print(f"largest single weight {w_is.max() * S_is:,.1f} times an equal weight; "
      f"top 1% of draws carry {srt[:S_is // 100].sum():.3f} of the weight")
```

The picture is a healthy one. The largest single weight is worth $9.1$ equal
weights rather than thousands, and the concentration curve in the right panel
bends above the diagonal without collapsing onto the axis: the top one percent of
draws carry $0.071$ of the total weight, against $0.01$ under equal weighting, so
no small set of draws dominates the average. The forty thousand weighted draws are
worth $11{,}855$ independent ones, a fraction $0.296$ of themselves, which is why
Lecture 3 could quote three parameters to three digits from a few seconds of array
arithmetic.

Nothing about that survives the models this course reaches by the middle of the
term. The vector autoregression of Lecture 6 carries around forty coefficients
and a covariance matrix, the stochastic volatility model of Lecture 12 extends
exactly the specification below with one latent volatility per month, several
hundred unknowns in total, and even this chapter's own working representation of
the Student-$t$ model, introduced in @sec-methodology, will have $442$ components.
A proposal has to cover the target everywhere at once, and the region a posterior
occupies shrinks relative to any fixed envelope as coordinates are added. The
experiment cannot be run directly on those models here, since none of them has
been built yet, but the rate at which a proposal loses its grip can be computed
exactly for a case where everything is known, and that is what @sec-problem does
before the repair is introduced. The question this lecture answers is what to do
when the number of parameters removes the option of proposing the whole vector
together, and the answer begins by asking how fast the option disappears.

## The problem: a fixed proposal degenerates geometrically in the dimension {#sec-problem}

### Result R-4.1: what a fixed proposal costs as parameters are added

Let the target $\pi$ and the proposal $q$ on $\mathbb{R}^k$ both factorise across
coordinates, $\pi(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{k}\pi_1(\theta_i)$ and
$q(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{k} q_1(\theta_i)$, with $q_1$ the same single-coordinate
proposal in every component. Write $w(\theta) = \pi(\theta)/q(\theta)$ for the
importance weight and

$$
\chi^2 = \int \frac{\pi_1(u)^2}{q_1(u)}\,du - 1 \;\ge\; 0
$$

for the chi-square divergence of $\pi_1$ from $q_1$, which is zero only if
$q_1 = \pi_1$. Then the relative variance of the weights and the effective sample
size fraction of $S$ draws satisfy

$$
\frac{\mathbb{E}_q[w^2]}{\left(\mathbb{E}_q[w]\right)^2} = \left(1 + \chi^2\right)^{k},
\qquad
\frac{S_{\text{eff}}}{S} \;\longrightarrow\; \left(1 + \chi^2\right)^{-k},
$$

and for rejection sampling with envelope constant
$M_k = \sup_\theta w(\theta) = M_1^{k}$ the acceptance probability is $M_1^{-k}$,
with $M_1 > 1$ unless $q_1 = \pi_1$ exactly. Both quantities decay geometrically
in $k$ at a rate fixed by the quality of the proposal in a single coordinate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Because both densities factorise, the weight factorises too,
$w(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^k w_1(\theta_i)$ with $w_1 = \pi_1/q_1$, and the
coordinates are independent under $q$. Expectations of products of independent
factors are products of expectations, so

$$
\mathbb{E}_q[w] = \left(\mathbb{E}_q[w_1]\right)^{k} = 1,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}_q[w^2] = \left(\mathbb{E}_q\!\left[w_1^2\right]\right)^{k},
$$

the first because $\mathbb{E}_q[w_1] = \int q_1 (\pi_1/q_1) = 1$. For a single
coordinate $\mathbb{E}_q[w_1^2] = \int \pi_1^2/q_1 = 1 + \chi^2$ by the definition
above, and $\chi^2 \ge 0$ with equality only when $\pi_1 = q_1$ almost everywhere,
since it is the variance of $w_1$ under $q$. Raising to the $k$-th power gives the
first display. The effective sample size of a self-normalised weighted sample,
defined in Lecture 3 as $S_{\text{eff}} = 1/\sum_s \bar w_s^2$ for normalised
weights $\bar w_s$, converges as $S \to \infty$ to
$S\,(\mathbb{E}_q[w])^2/\mathbb{E}_q[w^2]$ by the law of large numbers applied
separately to numerator and denominator, which is the second display.

For rejection sampling the envelope must satisfy $\pi \le M_k q$ everywhere, and
the smallest such constant is the supremum of $w$. A supremum of a product of
non-negative functions of separate variables is the product of the suprema, so
$M_k = M_1^k$ with $M_1 = \sup_u w_1(u)$, and $M_1 \ge \int q_1 w_1 = 1$ with
equality only in the degenerate case $q_1 = \pi_1$. The acceptance probability of
the rejection algorithm is $1/M_k$ when $\pi$ is a normalised density, which is
$M_1^{-k}$.

The factorised setting is the favourable one, not a worst case: it assumes the
proposal is equally good in every coordinate and that there is no dependence for
it to miss. Any mismatch in the correlation structure multiplies the same
constants further.
:::

A single number fixes the exponent. If $q_1$ is a $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$
proposal for a $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ coordinate, the integral above evaluates to
$1 + \chi^2 = \tau^2/\sqrt{2\tau^2 - 1}$ for $\tau^2 > 1/2$, so a proposal that is
ten percent too wide has $1 + \chi^2 = 1.0154$, a loss of one and a half percent
per coordinate that is invisible in one dimension and compounds to a factor of
nearly nine hundred once four hundred coordinates have been added. A proposal that
is fifty percent too wide has $1 + \chi^2 = 1.2027$, which is harmless at $k = 3$
and fatal long before $k$ reaches a hundred.

```{python}
ks = np.arange(1, 401)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
for tau, colour in zip([1.1, 1.25, 1.5], ["steelblue", "darkorange", "firebrick"]):
    chi = tau ** 2 / np.sqrt(2 * tau ** 2 - 1)
    axes[0].semilogy(ks, chi ** (-ks), color=colour,
                     label=fr"$\tau = {tau}$,  $1+\chi^2 = {chi:.4f}$")
    m1 = tau                                    # sup of the N(0,1)/N(0,tau^2) ratio
    axes[1].semilogy(ks, m1 ** (-ks), color=colour, label=fr"$\tau = {tau}$")
axes[0].axvline(3, color="black", ls=":"); axes[1].axvline(3, color="black", ls=":")
axes[0].set_xlabel("number of parameters k"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$S_{\rm eff}/S$")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8); axes[0].set_title("Importance sampling")
axes[1].set_xlabel("number of parameters k"); axes[1].set_ylabel("acceptance probability")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8); axes[1].set_title("Rejection sampling")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for tau in (1.1, 1.25, 1.5):
    chi = tau ** 2 / np.sqrt(2 * tau ** 2 - 1)
    print(f"tau {tau}: 1+chi^2 = {chi:.4f}; ESS/S at k=3 {chi ** -3:.4f}, "
          f"at k=40 {chi ** -40:.4g}, at k=442 {chi ** -442:.4g}; "
          f"acceptance at k=442 {tau ** -442:.4g}")
```

Both panels are straight lines on a log scale, which is the content of Result
R-4.1: the loss is geometric, not gradual. The dotted vertical line marks the
three parameters of @sec-motivation, where all three proposals are indeed
workable, the mildest of them keeping $0.955$ of its draws and the widest
$0.575$. At the forty parameters of Lecture 6 the same mildest proposal is down to
$0.54$ and the widest to $0.00062$, and at the $442$ components of the augmented
model below the three curves read $0.0012$, $5 \times 10^{-14}$ and
$4 \times 10^{-36}$. The rejection panel is worse for the same reason, because an
envelope has to dominate at every point rather than on average, so even the
mildest proposal accepts one candidate in $2 \times 10^{18}$ at $k = 442$, which
is not slow but unusable.

The diagnosis is therefore not that our particular proposal was badly chosen. It
is that the strategy of covering the whole parameter vector with one fixed density
is exponentially expensive in the number of parameters, and no amount of care
spent on $q_1$ changes the exponent. What can be changed is the dimension of the
object being proposed, and that is the repair.

## Methodology: latent scales and the Gibbs sampler {#sec-methodology}

If proposing $k$ coordinates at once is exponentially hard, propose one at a
time. The Gibbs sampler updates a single block of parameters from its full
conditional distribution, the conditional posterior of that block given the
current value of every other block and the data. Each such move is a
low-dimensional problem, often one-dimensional, so the exponent in Result R-4.1
never appears. The price is that consecutive draws are dependent, since each is
built from the last, and that the conditionals have to be distributions we can
draw from.

### Result R-4.2: the Gibbs sampler and its invariance

Let $\theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_B)$ be any partition of the parameter
vector into $B$ blocks, and suppose every full conditional
$\phi(\theta_b \mid \theta_{-b}, y)$ can be sampled. Starting from any
$\theta^{(0)}$ in the support, sweep $s = 1, 2, \dots$ draws

$$
\theta_b^{(s)} \;\sim\; \phi\!\left(\theta_b \;\Big|\;
\theta_1^{(s)}, \dots, \theta_{b-1}^{(s)},\,
\theta_{b+1}^{(s-1)}, \dots, \theta_B^{(s-1)},\, y\right),
\qquad b = 1, \dots, B,
$$

each block conditioning on the newest available value of every other block. The
resulting Markov chain leaves the joint posterior $\phi(\theta \mid y)$ invariant:
if $\theta^{(s-1)} \sim \phi(\cdot \mid y)$, then
$\theta^{(s)} \sim \phi(\cdot \mid y)$. The visiting order of the blocks is
irrelevant to this property, and nothing in it depends on $B$, on the dimension of
a block, or on the model.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Take one block update and suppose $\theta^{(s-1)} = (\theta_b, \theta_{-b})$ is a
draw from the joint posterior. Any joint density factors as
$\phi(\theta_b, \theta_{-b} \mid y) = \phi(\theta_b \mid \theta_{-b}, y)\,
\phi(\theta_{-b} \mid y)$. Since $\theta^{(s-1)}$ is a joint draw, its component
$\theta_{-b}$ is a draw from the marginal $\phi(\theta_{-b} \mid y)$. Discarding
$\theta_b$ and replacing it with a fresh draw $\theta_b'$ from
$\phi(\theta_b \mid \theta_{-b}, y)$ therefore produces a pair
$(\theta_b', \theta_{-b})$ whose density is the product of that marginal and that
conditional, which is the joint posterior again. One block update thus maps a
joint draw to a joint draw, and nothing in the argument used what the block was.

A sweep is the composition of $B$ such updates. If each of them maps the joint
posterior to itself, so does their composition, in any order, whether the order is
fixed or chosen at random at each sweep. In the language of Markov chains, each
update has transition kernel $P_b$ with
$\int \phi(\theta \mid y) P_b(\theta \to \theta')\, d\theta = \phi(\theta' \mid y)$,
and the sweep kernel $P = P_1 P_2 \cdots P_B$ inherits that property by applying
the individual ones in turn. Note what is not claimed: a single block update is
not reversible with respect to the posterior in the detailed-balance sense of
Lecture 5, and it does not need to be. Invariance of the composition is enough.
:::

Invariance says the posterior is a stationary distribution of the chain. It does
not by itself say the chain will find it from an arbitrary start, nor that
averages along one run converge. Three further properties close those gaps.
Irreducibility requires that the chain can reach any region of positive posterior
probability from any starting point in finitely many steps; it holds whenever the
full conditionals have support that does not depend on the conditioning values,
which is the case for every Normal, Gamma or fully supported discrete conditional
below. Aperiodicity rules out the chain cycling deterministically through a fixed
set of states, and with continuous conditionals it is automatic. Together with
invariance these give the chain a unique stationary distribution, which must be
the posterior, and convergence to it from any start. Convergence from an arbitrary
start is a limit statement, so the early draws are contaminated by the starting
value and are discarded as burn-in; there is no formula for how long that takes,
and the practical test is to start somewhere deliberately implausible and watch
the trace.

The law of large numbers of Lecture 3 assumed independent draws and does not
apply. What replaces it is the ergodic theorem: for an irreducible, aperiodic
chain with stationary distribution $\pi$ and any function $g$ with
$\mathbb{E}_\pi|g| < \infty$,

$$
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} g\!\left(\theta^{(s)}\right)
\;\longrightarrow\; \mathbb{E}_\pi[g(\theta)]
\qquad \text{almost surely as } S \to \infty,
$$

despite the dependence. Every posterior mean, credible interval and marginal
histogram reported from a chain is such an average, so this is the theorem that
licenses the whole output. What the dependence does change is the precision. For a
stationary chain the variance of the average is not $\gamma_0/S$ but

$$
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\bar g_S\right)
= \frac{1}{S}\left(\gamma_0 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{S-1}\left(1 - \frac{j}{S}\right)\gamma_j\right)
\;\longrightarrow\; \frac{S(0)}{S},
$$

where $\gamma_j$ is the autocovariance of $g(\theta^{(s)})$ at lag $j$ and $S(0)$
is the spectral density of that series at frequency zero. For a positively
autocorrelated chain $S(0) > \gamma_0$, so the naive standard error understates
the true one, sometimes by an order of magnitude. Rewriting the same quantity as
$\gamma_0/S_{\text{eff}}$ defines the effective sample size of a chain,

$$
S_{\text{eff}} = \frac{S}{1 + 2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\rho_j},
\qquad \rho_j = \gamma_j/\gamma_0,
$$

the number of independent draws the dependent run is worth. This is the same
quantity the importance weights of @sec-motivation were scored with, arrived at
from the other direction, and it is the currency of the comparison table at the
end of Lecture 5. Two further habits are worth separating. Subsampling the chain,
keeping every $m$-th draw so that what is kept is nearly independent, makes the
naive standard error usable again but throws away information, so a thinned
average is less precise than the full one, not more. Running several chains from
dispersed starting values is different in kind, because the chains never
communicate, and disagreement between chains started far apart is the most
convincing evidence of non-convergence there is.

### Result R-4.3: the scale mixture and the full conditionals it creates

The Student-$t$ posterior does not look like it has recognisable full
conditionals, and taken at face value it does not. The move that creates them is
data augmentation: add one unobserved scale per observation, chosen so that
conditioning on it turns the Student-$t$ into a Normal model with known unequal
weights. The identity is stated for a single observation with arbitrary location
and scale, and the conditionals for a general linear model with $n$ observations
and $k$ regressors, because that is the form the exercise session, Lecture 6 and
Lecture 12 all reuse.

::: {.callout-important}
## Result R-4.3

Mixing a Normal over a Gamma scale gives a Student-$t$: if $w > 0$ has density
$\text{Gamma}(\tfrac{\nu}{2}, \tfrac{\nu}{2})$ in the shape-rate parameterisation
and $x \mid w \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/w)$, then marginally
$x \sim t_\nu(\mu, \sigma)$, with density

$$
f(x) = \frac{\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{\nu+1}{2}\big)}
            {\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{\nu}{2}\big)\sqrt{\pi\nu}\,\sigma}
\left[1 + \frac{1}{\nu}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^{\!2}\right]^{-(\nu+1)/2}.
$$

Apply it to every observation of $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $X$ an
$n \times k$ design matrix, $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2/w_t)$
independently, $W = \text{diag}(w_1, \dots, w_n)$, and independent priors
$\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(b_0, B_0)$ and
$\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$. The four full conditionals are

$$
\beta \mid \sigma^2, w, y \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(b_1, B_1), \qquad
B_1 = \left(B_0^{-1} + \frac{X^\top W X}{\sigma^2}\right)^{-1}, \qquad
b_1 = B_1\left(B_0^{-1}b_0 + \frac{X^\top W y}{\sigma^2}\right),
$$

$$
\sigma^2 \mid \beta, w, y \;\sim\; \text{IG}\!\left(\alpha_0 + \frac{n}{2},\;
\delta_0 + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{n} w_t (y_t - x_t^\top\beta)^2\right),
$$

$$
w_t \mid \beta, \sigma^2, \nu, y \;\overset{\text{ind}}{\sim}\;
\text{Gamma}\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2},\; \frac{\nu + z_t^2}{2}\right),
\qquad z_t = \frac{y_t - x_t^\top\beta}{\sigma},
$$

$$
\phi(\nu \mid w) \;\propto\; \phi(\nu)\,
\left[\frac{(\nu/2)^{\nu/2}}{\Gamma(\nu/2)}\right]^{n}
\exp\!\left\{\frac{\nu}{2}\left(\sum_{t=1}^n \log w_t - \sum_{t=1}^n w_t\right)\right\},
$$

the last of which is not a standard family for any of the usual priors
$\phi(\nu)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation of the mixture identity

Write $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ and integrate the joint density of $x$ and $w$ over
$w$. The conditional density of $x$ contributes a factor $w^{1/2}$ and an
exponential in $w$, and the Gamma density of $w$ contributes $w^{\nu/2 - 1}$ and a
second exponential in $w$, so the two powers and the two exponents collect:

$$
f(x, w) =
\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{w}{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{w z^2}{2}\right)}_{x \mid w}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{(\nu/2)^{\nu/2}}{\Gamma(\nu/2)} w^{\nu/2 - 1}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\nu w}{2}\right)}_{w}
\;\propto\; w^{\frac{\nu+1}{2} - 1}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{w}{2}\left(\nu + z^2\right)\right].
$$

As a function of $w$ this is the kernel of a $\text{Gamma}\big(\tfrac{\nu+1}{2},
\tfrac{\nu + z^2}{2}\big)$ density, so its integral is the reciprocal of that
density's normalising constant,

$$
\int_0^\infty w^{\frac{\nu+1}{2} - 1} e^{-\frac{w}{2}(\nu + z^2)}\, dw
= \Gamma\!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)
\left(\frac{\nu + z^2}{2}\right)^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}} .
$$

Restoring the constants carried along the way, and writing
$(\nu + z^2)^{-(\nu+1)/2} = \nu^{-(\nu+1)/2}(1 + z^2/\nu)^{-(\nu+1)/2}$, gives
exactly the Student-$t$ density in the statement, with the powers of two and of
$\nu$ cancelling against the $(\nu/2)^{\nu/2}$ from the Gamma prior and the
$\Gamma(\nu/2)$ surviving in the denominator. Equivalently, with
$\lambda^2 = 1/w$, the mixing variable is inverse-Gamma,
$\lambda^2 \sim \text{IG}(\tfrac{\nu}{2}, \tfrac{\nu}{2})$, and
$x = \mu + \lambda\sigma u$ with $u \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ independent of
$\lambda$. The same computation read in the other direction, with $z$ fixed and
$w$ unknown, is the full conditional of $w$ below: the integrand is already a
Gamma kernel in $w$, which is why no further work is needed there.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation of the four full conditionals

The augmented likelihood, as a function of all four blocks, is

$$
f(y \mid \beta, \sigma^2, w) \;\propto\;
\sigma^{-n}\prod_{t=1}^n w_t^{1/2}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{t=1}^n w_t (y_t - x_t^\top\beta)^2\right\}
= \sigma^{-n}|W|^{1/2}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(y - X\beta)^\top W (y - X\beta)}{2\sigma^2}\right\}.
$$

For $\beta$, hold $\sigma^2$ and $w$ fixed. Only the exponential involves $\beta$,
and together with the Normal prior the exponent is

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{(y - X\beta)^\top W (y-X\beta)}{\sigma^2}
+ (\beta - b_0)^\top B_0^{-1}(\beta - b_0)\right]
= -\frac{1}{2}\left[\beta^\top\! \left(B_0^{-1} + \frac{X^\top W X}{\sigma^2}\right)\!\beta
- 2\beta^\top\!\left(B_0^{-1}b_0 + \frac{X^\top W y}{\sigma^2}\right)\right] + c,
$$

with $c$ free of $\beta$. This is a quadratic form in $\beta$ with matrix
$B_1^{-1} = B_0^{-1} + \sigma^{-2}X^\top W X$ and linear term
$B_1^{-1}b_1 = B_0^{-1}b_0 + \sigma^{-2}X^\top W y$. Completing the square, that is
adding and subtracting $b_1^\top B_1^{-1} b_1$, turns it into
$-\tfrac{1}{2}(\beta - b_1)^\top B_1^{-1}(\beta - b_1)$ plus a further constant,
which is the kernel of the stated Normal. The location-only case used in this
chapter is $X = \iota$, the vector of ones and $k = 1$, where
$X^\top W X = \sum_t w_t$ and $X^\top W y = \sum_t w_t y_t$, so the posterior
precision is $1/s_0^2 + \sum_t w_t/\sigma^2$ and the posterior mean is the
precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the weighted sample mean
$\sum_t w_t y_t / \sum_t w_t$.

For $\sigma^2$, hold $\beta$ and $w$ fixed and collect powers. The likelihood
contributes $(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}$ and an exponential in $1/\sigma^2$, the prior
contributes $(\sigma^2)^{-(\alpha_0+1)}\exp(-\delta_0/\sigma^2)$, so

$$
\phi(\sigma^2 \mid \beta, w, y) \;\propto\;
(\sigma^2)^{-\left(\alpha_0 + \frac{n}{2}\right) - 1}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\left(\delta_0
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\textstyle\sum_t w_t (y_t - x_t^\top\beta)^2\right)\right\},
$$

which is the inverse-Gamma kernel $(\sigma^2)^{-a-1}e^{-d/\sigma^2}$ with the
stated $a$ and $d$. No completing the square is needed because the exponent is
already linear in $1/\sigma^2$.

For $w_t$, hold everything else fixed. Observation $t$ contributes
$w_t^{1/2}\exp(-w_t z_t^2/2)$ and the mixing prior contributes
$w_t^{\nu/2 - 1}\exp(-\nu w_t/2)$, and these are the two factors already
multiplied together in the derivation of the mixture identity:

$$
\phi(w_t \mid \cdot) \;\propto\; w_t^{\frac{\nu+1}{2}-1}
\exp\!\left\{-\frac{w_t(\nu + z_t^2)}{2}\right\},
$$

a Gamma kernel with shape $(\nu+1)/2$ and rate $(\nu + z_t^2)/2$. Nothing links
$w_t$ to $w_s$ for $s \neq t$ once the parameters are fixed, so the $n$
conditionals are independent and can be drawn in one vectorised call. The
conditional mean is $(\nu+1)/(\nu + z_t^2)$, which falls towards zero as the
standardised residual grows.

For $\nu$, hold $w$ fixed. The data enter only through $w$, since given $w$ the
likelihood of $y$ does not involve $\nu$ at all. Multiplying the $n$ Gamma
densities and keeping only factors containing $\nu$ gives
$[(\nu/2)^{\nu/2}/\Gamma(\nu/2)]^n \exp\{\tfrac{\nu}{2}(\sum_t \log w_t - \sum_t w_t)\}$
times the prior, which is the statement. Two features of it matter. It depends on
the $n$ latent variables only through the two sufficient statistics
$\sum_t \log w_t$ and $\sum_t w_t$, so evaluating it costs nothing extra as $n$
grows. And it matches no standard family, because $\nu$ appears both inside a
Gamma function and in an exponent, so this block cannot be drawn directly.
:::

The identity is exact, not an approximation, and it says something interpretable.
A Student-$t$ return is a Normal return whose variance was drawn at random before
the return was drawn: months with a small $w_t$ are months drawn from a wide
Normal, which is what a crash is under this model. The parameter $\nu$ governs how
dispersed those scales are, since $\text{Var}(w) = 2/\nu$, so a small $\nu$ makes
the monthly variances very unequal and a large $\nu$ pins every $w_t$ near one and
returns the model to a single Gaussian. Treating the $n$ scales as parameters
rather than integrating them away grows the parameter vector from $3$ to $n+3$
components, which sounds like a step backwards and is not. The marginal posterior
of $(\mu, \sigma, \nu)$ implied by the augmented model is exactly the posterior of
Lecture 3, because integrating each $w_t$ back out returns the Student-$t$
likelihood we started from, and the $w_t$ are conditionally independent of each
other, so the $n$ extra blocks cost $n$ scalar Gamma draws in one vectorised line.
Result R-4.1 charged for dimension only because the whole vector had to be
proposed at once; Result R-4.2 never proposes more than one block, so the same
$442$ components are now free.

Three of the four blocks are therefore standard, and the two moves used are the
ones that have appeared in every conjugate calculation of the course so far:
completing the square when the exponent is quadratic in the unknown, and
collecting exponents when it is linear in the reciprocal of the unknown. The
fourth block, $\nu$, is the obstacle, and there are three workable responses. Fix
$\nu$ at a value chosen in advance, which throws away the question that motivated
the model. Replace the direct draw by a Metropolis-Hastings step, which is
Lecture 5 and is the general answer. Or discretise: evaluate the conditional on a
fine grid over the prior's support $(2, 50]$, normalise, and draw from the
resulting discrete distribution. This last option, the griddy Gibbs step, needs no
tuning and is exact up to the grid spacing, which is why we use it here; at a
spacing of $0.04$ the discretisation error in $\mathbb{E}[\nu \mid r]$ is far
below the simulation error we will report.

## Data: monthly US market excess returns, 1990 to 2026 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the one Lectures 3 and 5 also use, the monthly
Fama-French factor file `data/ff_factors_monthly.parquet` from the Kenneth French
data library. The column `mkt_rf` is the excess return on the value-weighted US
market portfolio over the one-month Treasury bill, and the window is January 1990
to July 2026, $n = 439$ months, chosen in Lecture 3 as the period over which a
single premium is worth entertaining.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(100 * r, bins=40, density=True, color="steelblue", alpha=0.7,
        label="439 monthly excess returns")
xg = np.linspace(-25, 20, 400)
ax.plot(xg, stats.norm(100 * r.mean(), 100 * r.std(ddof=1)).pdf(xg), "k--", lw=1.5,
        label="Normal with the same mean and sd")
ax.set_xlabel("monthly market excess return, percent"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Too many quiet months and too many extreme ones")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{n} months, {sample.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {sample.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"mean {r.mean():.5f}, sd {r.std(ddof=1):.5f}, "
      f"skewness {stats.skew(r):.3f}, excess kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(r):.3f}")
print(f"worst {r.min():.4f} ({sample.index[r.argmin()]:%Y-%m}), "
      f"best {r.max():.4f} ({sample.index[r.argmax()]:%Y-%m})")
print(f"months beyond three sample sd: {(np.abs(r - r.mean()) > 3 * r.std(ddof=1)).sum()}, "
      f"expected under a Normal {439 * 2 * stats.norm.sf(3):.2f}")
```

The histogram is the reason the model of Lecture 3 has a $\nu$ in it at all. The
Normal density with the same mean and standard deviation, drawn as the dashed
line, is too low in the middle and too thin at both ends: the sample has an excess
kurtosis of $1.03$ and a skewness of $-0.55$, and three months lie more than three
sample standard deviations from the mean where a Normal would produce about one.
The worst month is October 2008 at $-17.20$ percent and the best April 2020 at
$13.60$ percent, and the whole
argument of this chapter is that a sensible estimate of the average premium should
not let those two months count as much as May 2013 does.

Nothing about the model, the priors or the window changes from Lecture 3:
$\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, s_0^2)$, $\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$
and $\nu - 2$ exponential with mean $\bar\nu$ truncated to $(0, 48]$, at
$m_0 = 0$, $s_0 = 0.01$, $\alpha_0 = 3$, $\delta_0 = 0.0032$ and $\bar\nu = 10$.
As there, $\sigma$ is the scale and not the standard deviation of a return, which
is $\sigma\sqrt{\nu/(\nu-2)}$. Lecture 3's reference answer on a
$64 \times 64 \times 96$ grid is carried in as `grid_mean` and `grid_sd` above and
serves as the ground truth for everything below.

## Empirical analysis: the equity premium by Gibbs sampling {#sec-empirical}

Before running the sampler it is worth checking the representation that makes it
possible, since everything downstream depends on Result R-4.3 being an identity
rather than an approximation.

```{python}
mu_c, sig_c, nu_c = 0.009, 0.038, 8.0
w_chk = rng.gamma(nu_c / 2, 2.0 / nu_c, size=200_000)
x_chk = mu_c + sig_c * rng.standard_normal(200_000) / np.sqrt(w_chk)

x0 = 0.02
mix_density = np.mean(stats.norm(mu_c, sig_c / np.sqrt(w_chk)).pdf(x0))
print(f"mixture density at x = {x0}: Monte Carlo {mix_density:.4f}, "
      f"Student-t {stats.t(df=nu_c, loc=mu_c, scale=sig_c).pdf(x0):.4f}")
print(f"variance of the mixing weight: sample {w_chk.var(ddof=1):.4f}, "
      f"theoretical 2/nu = {2/nu_c:.4f}")

grid_x = np.linspace(-0.2, 0.2, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(w_chk, bins=80, density=True, color="steelblue", alpha=0.7)
axes[0].axvline(1.0, color="black", ls=":")
axes[0].set_xlim(0, 3); axes[0].set_xlabel(r"mixing weight $w$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("density"); axes[0].set_title(r"$w \sim$ Gamma$(\nu/2, \nu/2)$, $\nu = 8$")
axes[1].hist(x_chk, bins=300, density=True, color="steelblue", alpha=0.55,
             label="Normal mixed over w")
axes[1].plot(grid_x, stats.t(df=nu_c, loc=mu_c, scale=sig_c).pdf(grid_x), "k--", lw=1.5,
             label=r"$t_\nu(\mu,\sigma)$")
axes[1].set_xlim(-0.2, 0.2); axes[1].set_xlabel("return"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=9)
axes[1].set_title("The mixture is the Student-t")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The left panel shows the mixing distribution: most months get a weight near one,
but the right tail of $w$ reaches three and the left tail comes arbitrarily close
to zero, which is where the fat tails of the return come from. The right panel
confirms the identity, the simulated mixture lying on the Student-$t$ density
across the whole range including the tails, and the printed densities agreeing to
four significant figures at a return of two percent. The printed variance of the
weights matches the theoretical $2/\nu = 0.25$, which is the formal version of the
same point: the smaller the degrees of freedom, the more unequal the monthly
variances the model is willing to entertain.

The sampler is the four conditionals of Result R-4.3 in a loop, with $X = \iota$
and $k = 1$ so that the $\beta$ block is the scalar $\mu$. The weights are drawn
in one vectorised call, and the $\nu$ block is the griddy step, whose grid and
prior term are built once outside the loop. We start the chain at $\mu = 0$, a
monthly premium of zero, $\sigma = 0.045$, well above the plausible scale, and
$\nu = 40$, essentially a Normal model, so that the burn-in is visible rather than
assumed.

```{python}
nu_grid = np.arange(2.02, 50.001, 0.04)
a_grid = nu_grid / 2.0
log_prior_nu = nu_const - (nu_grid - nu_lo) / nu_mean
gamma_const = n * (a_grid * np.log(a_grid) - gammaln(a_grid))


def gibbs(n_sweeps, burn, rng, mu=0.0, sigma2=0.045 ** 2, nu=40.0):
    """Gibbs sampler for the Student-t location-scale model via scale mixing."""
    kept = np.empty((n_sweeps - burn, 3))
    w_sum, w = np.zeros(n), np.ones(n)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for s in range(n_sweeps):
        prec = 1.0 / s_0 ** 2 + w.sum() / sigma2                  # mu | sigma^2, w, r
        mean = (m_0 / s_0 ** 2 + (w * r).sum() / sigma2) / prec
        mu = rng.normal(mean, 1.0 / np.sqrt(prec))

        ssr = (w * (r - mu) ** 2).sum()                           # sigma^2 | mu, w, r
        sigma2 = 1.0 / rng.gamma(alpha_0 + n / 2, 1.0 / (delta_0 + 0.5 * ssr))

        z2 = (r - mu) ** 2 / sigma2                               # w | mu, sigma^2, nu, r
        w = rng.gamma((nu + 1) / 2, 2.0 / (nu + z2))

        S1, S2 = np.log(w).sum(), w.sum()                         # nu | w, on the grid
        log_p = gamma_const + (a_grid - 1.0) * S1 - a_grid * S2 + log_prior_nu
        p = np.exp(log_p - log_p.max()); p /= p.sum()
        nu = rng.choice(nu_grid, p=p)

        if s >= burn:
            kept[s - burn] = (mu, np.sqrt(sigma2), nu)
            w_sum += w
    return kept, w_sum / (n_sweeps - burn), time.perf_counter() - t0


burn, n_sweeps = 2_000, 62_000
draws, w_mean, gibbs_secs = gibbs(n_sweeps, burn, rng)
print(f"{draws.shape[0]:,} sweeps kept after {burn:,} burn-in, "
      f"{gibbs_secs:.1f} seconds, {n + 3} blocks updated per sweep")
```

Sixty thousand sweeps of a model with four hundred and forty-two unknowns take
about nine seconds, which is the practical case for Gibbs sampling in one line:
every operation inside the loop is a draw from a named distribution, and the
expensive-looking latent block is a single vectorised call. Nothing in the loop
evaluates the Student-$t$ density, and nothing in it needs a proposal, an envelope
constant or a tuning parameter, which is the contrast with @sec-motivation. The
trace plots show what the chain did with those sweeps.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True)
labels = [r"$\mu$", r"$\sigma$", r"$\nu$"]
show = 6_000
for j, (ax, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes, labels)):
    ax.plot(np.arange(show), draws[:show, j], lw=0.4, color="steelblue")
    ax.axhline(grid_mean[j], color="black", ls=":", label="grid value, Lecture 3")
    ax.set_ylabel(lab)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[2].set_xlabel("sweep after burn-in")
fig.suptitle("Gibbs traces for the three parameters of interest")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

All three traces move in a stationary band around the Lecture 3 grid values from
the first kept sweep onwards, so the two thousand discarded sweeps were more than
enough to erase the deliberately poor start. The three traces are visibly
different in character. The trace for $\mu$ is a thin noisy band that looks almost
like independent draws, while the traces for $\sigma$ and especially for $\nu$
show slow excursions lasting hundreds of sweeps, the visual signature of high
autocorrelation, and that difference is measured next.

```{python}
def acf(x, max_lag):
    x = x - x.mean(); m = x.size; v = np.dot(x, x) / m
    return np.array([np.dot(x[:m - k], x[k:]) / m / v for k in range(max_lag + 1)])


def ess(x, max_lag=2_000):
    """Effective sample size, Geyer's initial positive sequence."""
    a = acf(x, max_lag); s = 0.0
    for k in range(1, max_lag - 1, 2):
        if a[k] + a[k + 1] < 0:
            break
        s += a[k] + a[k + 1]
    return x.size / (1.0 + 2.0 * s)


post_mean = draws.mean(axis=0)
post_sd = draws.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
ess_gibbs = np.array([ess(draws[:, j]) for j in range(3)])
mcse = post_sd / np.sqrt(ess_gibbs)
table = pd.DataFrame({"Gibbs mean": post_mean, "grid mean": grid_mean,
                      "Gibbs sd": post_sd, "grid sd": grid_sd,
                      "ESS": ess_gibbs, "MCSE": mcse,
                      "|error|/MCSE": np.abs(post_mean - grid_mean) / mcse},
                     index=names)
print(table.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.6f}"))
p_thick = (draws[:, 2] < 10).mean()
print(f"\nP(nu < 10 | r) = {p_thick:.4f} (MCSE {np.sqrt(p_thick*(1-p_thick)/ess_gibbs[2]):.4f})"
      f"   Lecture 3 exact draws: 0.7567")
print(f"annualised premium 12 * E[mu | r] = {12 * post_mean[0]:.4f}, "
      f"implied monthly return sd "
      f"{post_mean[1] * np.sqrt(post_mean[2] / (post_mean[2] - 2)):.4f} "
      f"vs sample {r.std(ddof=1):.4f}")
print(f"ESS per second: " + ", ".join(f"{nm} {e/gibbs_secs:,.0f}"
                                      for nm, e in zip(names, ess_gibbs)))
```

The two helpers are the estimator of the effective sample size defined in
@sec-methodology: the sample autocorrelation at each lag, and Geyer's initial
positive sequence rule, which truncates the sum over lags at the first pair of
consecutive autocorrelations whose sum turns negative. Both are reused unchanged
in Lecture 5, so the comparison at the end of that chapter prices every sampler
with the same instrument.

The table is the validation this chapter exists for. Every posterior mean lands
within one Monte Carlo standard error of the grid value of Lecture 3, the largest
discrepancy being half a standard error, and the posterior standard deviations
agree to within a tenth of a percent for $\mu$ and $\sigma$ and to about three
percent for $\nu$, so a Markov chain that never
evaluated the Student-$t$ likelihood at all, and never computed a normalising
constant, has reproduced a posterior obtained in Lecture 3 by two independent
routes, deterministic quadrature and exact rejection sampling. The posterior
probability of genuinely thick tails comes out at $0.7429$ against the $0.7567$ of
Lecture 3's exact draws, a gap of $0.0138$ against a Monte Carlo standard error of
$0.0156$, which is the right order for a probability read off the most slowly
mixing of the three parameters.

The economics is Lecture 3's and survives the change of method. The annualised
premium at the posterior mean is just under eleven percent, well above twelve
times the sample average of $0.745$ percent a month, because the $t$ model reads
2008 and 2020 as tail draws rather than as evidence for a lower mean. The implied
monthly return standard deviation is close to the sample standard deviation of
$0.0439$, so the fat tails are not bought at the cost of overall spread, and the
degrees of freedom near nine put the market firmly outside the Gaussian world.

The effective sample sizes are the new information. Sixty thousand sweeps are
worth about ten thousand eight hundred independent draws for $\mu$ but only around
fifteen hundred for $\sigma$ and eight hundred for $\nu$, a spread of more than an
order of magnitude within one chain. The autocorrelation functions show where that
comes from.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
for j, colour in zip(range(3), ["steelblue", "darkorange", "firebrick"]):
    axes[0].plot(np.arange(201), acf(draws[:, j], 200), lw=1.2, color=colour,
                 label=f"{names[j]}  (ESS {ess_gibbs[j]:,.0f})")
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("lag (sweeps)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("autocorrelation")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8); axes[0].set_title("Dependence within the chain")
axes[1].scatter(draws[::20, 1], draws[::20, 2], s=4, alpha=0.15, color="steelblue")
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"$\sigma$"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\nu$"); axes[1].set_ylim(2, 30)
axes[1].set_title(r"Joint posterior of $(\sigma, \nu)$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

a_mu, a_nu = acf(draws[:, 0], 200), acf(draws[:, 2], 200)
print(f"autocorrelation of mu:  lag 1 {a_mu[1]:.3f}, lag 5 {a_mu[5]:.3f}, "
      f"lag 20 {a_mu[20]:.3f}")
print(f"autocorrelation of nu:  lag 1 {a_nu[1]:.3f}, lag 20 {a_nu[20]:.3f}, "
      f"lag 50 {a_nu[50]:.3f}, lag 100 {a_nu[100]:.3f}")
print(f"correlation between the sigma and nu draws: "
      f"{np.corrcoef(draws[:, 1], draws[:, 2])[0, 1]:.3f}")
```

The printed autocorrelations put numbers on the two shapes. That of $\mu$ is gone
within a handful of lags, while that of $\nu$ starts close to one and decays so
slowly that it is still clearly positive fifty lags later. The right panel
explains it, and it is the same curved ridge
Lecture 3 plotted from its rejection draws: $\sigma$ and $\nu$ are strongly
dependent, because a model with thicker tails needs a smaller scale to fit the
same returns. A Gibbs sampler moves along one coordinate at a time, so along a
ridge tilted away from the axes it can only take small steps, and the correlation
is transmitted through the latent weights as well, since a sweep that draws a
small $\nu$ produces more dispersed weights, which produces a smaller weighted sum
of squares, which pulls $\sigma$ down at the next sweep.

The mixing variables were introduced as a computational device, and they are also
the most directly interpretable output of the model. The posterior mean of $w_t$
is the weight the model gives month $t$ when it estimates the premium and the
scale: a month with $w_t$ near one is an ordinary month, while a month with $w_t$
near a tenth counts for about a tenth of an ordinary month. Nothing told the
sampler which months were unusual.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
ax.plot(sample.index, w_mean, lw=0.9, color="steelblue")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.axhline(1.0, color="black", ls=":")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel(r"posterior mean of $w_t$ (log scale)")
ax.set_title("How much each month counts under the fitted Student-t model")
worst = np.argsort(w_mean)[:6]
for i in worst[:3]:
    ax.annotate(f"{sample.index[i]:%b %Y}", (sample.index[i], w_mean[i]),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, -2), fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(pd.DataFrame({"month": sample.index[worst].strftime("%Y-%m"),
                    "excess return": r[worst],
                    "posterior mean w_t": w_mean[worst]}).round(4).to_string(index=False))
print(f"median weight {np.median(w_mean):.4f}, smallest {w_mean.min():.4f}, "
      f"months with weight below 0.6: {(w_mean < 0.6).sum()} of {n}")
```

The series of weights is a list of financial history written by the residuals
alone. The six most heavily discounted months are October 2008, August 1998, the
crash and the rebound of March and April 2020, November 2000 and November 2020,
each counting for between $0.30$ and $0.52$ of an ordinary month, and the median
month sits at $1.06$, slightly above one, because the weights must average out against the
discounted extremes. Two of the six are large positive returns: the model
down-weights surprise in either direction, which is what a symmetric scale mixture
must do, and is a reminder that $\nu$ measures tail thickness rather than crash
risk specifically. That is what the Student-$t$ model does that a Gaussian one
cannot. Rather than deleting outliers or letting them drag the estimates, it
down-weights them by an amount the data themselves determine through $\nu$, and
the down-weighting falls out of one Gamma draw per month.

The three outputs belong together as one answer to the risk desk's question. The
expected monthly excess return is $0.0091$ with a posterior standard deviation of
$0.0020$, so the annualised premium is $10.9$ percent and one posterior standard
deviation either side of it runs from $8.5$ to $13.4$ percent, a wider range than
a point estimate suggests and a narrower one than the monthly volatility alone
would imply. An ordinary month has scale $0.0378$, and the return
standard deviation the model implies, $0.0431$, is what the desk should use for a
quiet month rather than the sample figure of $0.0439$, which is inflated by the
same seventeen months the weights discount. The degrees of freedom carry the tail
risk: a posterior mean of $8.6$ with $0.74$ of the mass below ten says the market
is firmly non-Gaussian, and it is this parameter, not the scale, that decides how
often the desk should expect a month like October 2008. That all three numbers
came out of a chain whose every step was a draw from a named distribution, with no
tuning constant anywhere, is the practical argument for the method.

## Discussion: fast blocks, a slow ridge, and a conditional with no name {#sec-discussion}

The answer to the question Lecture 3 posed is unchanged, and that is the first
thing to say: the posterior mean premium is about $0.9$ percent a month with a
posterior standard deviation of $0.2$, the scale is $0.038$, and the degrees of
freedom sit near nine with substantial mass below ten. What has changed is how the
answer was obtained. No proposal density was written down, no envelope constant
was searched for, and the exponential penalty of Result R-4.1 never appeared even
though the working parameter vector had $442$ components. The check against
something already known is the table of @sec-empirical: every mean is within one
Monte Carlo standard error of Lecture 3's grid, computed by quadrature on a
$393{,}216$-point grid and confirmed there by exact rejection draws. Three
independent routes to the same three numbers is the strongest evidence a
simulation method can be given, and it is worth having precisely because from
Lecture 6 onwards no reference answer will exist.

The cost is dependence, and it is not evenly spread. The effective sample sizes
say that a sweep is worth about a sixth of an independent draw for $\mu$ and about
a hundredth for $\nu$. The mechanism is the geometry of @sec-empirical's right
panel, and it is easiest to see in a two-dimensional Normal posterior with
correlation $\rho$ between standardised coordinates, whose conditionals are
$\theta_1 \mid \theta_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\rho\theta_2, 1 - \rho^2)$ and
symmetrically, obtained by completing the square in the bivariate Normal exponent
exactly as in Result R-4.3. A full sweep multiplies the deviation from the mean by
$\rho^2$ in expectation, so the chain's autocorrelation at lag one is $\rho^2$ and
mixing degrades quadratically as the ridge sharpens.

```{python}
#| label: fig-gibbs-ridge
#| fig-cap: "Coordinate-wise updates on a Normal posterior with weak and strong correlation. Both panels use exact full conditionals; only the geometry differs."
geom_rng = np.random.default_rng(410)
g = np.linspace(-3, 3, 150)
A, B = np.meshgrid(g, g)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, rho in zip(axes, [0.2, 0.95]):
    dens = np.exp(-(A ** 2 - 2 * rho * A * B + B ** 2) / (2 * (1 - rho ** 2)))
    ax.contour(A, B, dens, levels=[0.05, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8], colors="#9babb7")
    point, path = np.array([-2.0, -2.0]), [np.array([-2.0, -2.0])]
    for _ in range(45):
        point[0] = geom_rng.normal(rho * point[1], np.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2))
        path.append(point.copy())
        point[1] = geom_rng.normal(rho * point[0], np.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2))
        path.append(point.copy())
    path = np.array(path)
    ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], lw=0.8, color="#527a99")
    ax.set(title=fr"$\rho = {rho}$, lag-1 autocorrelation $\rho^2 = {rho**2:.2f}$",
           xlabel=r"$\theta_1$", xlim=(-3, 3), ylim=(-3, 3))
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\theta_2$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

At $\rho = 0.2$ the chain crosses the posterior in a few sweeps. At $\rho = 0.95$
it edges along the ridge in small horizontal and vertical steps, and the same
number of sweeps covers a fraction of the distribution, even though every single
draw is an exact draw from an exact conditional. The remedies are structural
rather than numerical: draw correlated parameters in one block where the joint
conditional is available, as the vector $\beta$ block of Result R-4.3 does for all
$k$ regression coefficients at once; reparameterise so that the ridge lines up
with the axes; or move to a sampler that proposes joint moves. Running the chain
longer works too, and is the most expensive of the four.

The binding limitation is not speed. Result R-4.2 requires every full conditional
to be a distribution we can draw from, and this chapter has already met one that
is not. The conditional of $\nu$ belongs to no standard family, and the grid we
used to get around that works only because $\nu$ is a bounded scalar. It does not
generalise: a block that is five-dimensional cannot be gridded at any affordable
cost, by exactly the counting argument of Result R-4.1, and a block whose
conditional support depends on the other blocks cannot be gridded safely at all.
Without a conditionally conjugate structure there is no Gibbs step to take, and
that is the breakdown Lecture 5 starts from. What replaces the direct draw is an
algorithm that only needs to evaluate a conditional density rather than sample it,
and that can be dropped into a Gibbs sweep for the one offending block while every
other block keeps its exact draw. That algorithm is Metropolis-Hastings, and
Lecture 5 develops it on this same posterior, this time with no latent variables
at all, before adding gradient information through Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and
NUTS, and closes with a table that prices every method in Lectures 3 to 5 in
effective draws per second on this identical problem.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 4 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/04-gibbs-sampling.qmd) works through them and adds
the lab.

1. By hand. Take the two-block Gibbs sampler for a bivariate Normal posterior with
   unit variances and correlation $\rho$. Derive both full conditionals by
   completing the square, show that a full sweep satisfies
   $\mathbb{E}[\theta^{(s)} \mid \theta^{(s-1)}] = \rho^2 \theta^{(s-1)}$, and
   deduce the lag-one autocorrelation and the effective sample size of a run of
   length $S$. State what happens as $\rho \to 1$ and relate it to the
   $(\sigma, \nu)$ ridge of @sec-empirical.

2. Computational. Replace the griddy step for $\nu$ in the sampler of
   @sec-empirical by a grid of spacing $0.5$, $0.1$ and $0.01$ over the same
   support, and report $\mathbb{E}[\nu \mid r]$ and its Monte Carlo standard error
   for each. Say at which spacing the discretisation error becomes visible against
   the simulation error, and explain why the same experiment in five dimensions
   would be infeasible using Result R-4.1.

3. On real data. Fit the Student-$t$ regression of Result R-4.3 with $k = 4$,
   taking the banks industry portfolio of Lecture 2 as $y$ and the three
   Fama-French factors as regressors, using the same monthly file. Report the
   posterior of $\beta$, the posterior of $\nu$, and the six months with the
   smallest posterior mean weight. Compare the coefficient on the market factor
   with the Normal-error answer of Lecture 2 and explain the difference in one
   paragraph.

Exercise 1 is the one to attempt before the session, since the algebra is short
and it is the quantitative version of the picture in @sec-discussion. Exercises 2
and 3 reuse the code of @sec-empirical with the $\beta$ block restored to its
general form.

## Reading and references

The Gibbs sampler and its invariance in @sec-methodology follow UPM Class 3 and
Case 2, with the block-composition argument as given there; UPM Class 5 gives the
regression version reused in Exercise 3, and Case 4 the latent allocation
variables that Lecture 11 returns to. The scale mixture representation and the
four full conditionals of Result R-4.3 follow Chapter 3 of Bauwens' lecture notes
and Geweke (1993), stated here for a general design matrix rather than for a
location model. The degeneracy of a fixed proposal in Result R-4.1 is standard and
is the same chi-square divergence bound that scored the importance weights in
Lecture 3; Chapter 9 of Owen and Section 10.2 of Gelman et al. give the longer
version. Greenberg (2008), Sections 7.1 and 8.1, connects Gibbs sampling to
regression, and Section 7.4 discusses burn-in, thinning and multiple chains in the
terms used in @sec-methodology. The UPM materials are by Audronė Virbickaitė and
Martina Zaharieva, adapted to this course's notation and weekly sequence.

Where the sources write the mixing variable as $\lambda_t^2 = 1/w_t$ with
$\lambda_t^2 \sim \text{IG}_2(\nu, \nu)$, or the error precision as
$h = 1/\sigma^2 \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha_0, 1/\delta_0)$, the objects are the ones
used here with the variable inverted; $\nu_0 = 2\alpha_0$ and $s_0 = 2\delta_0$
convert the $\text{IG}_2$ parameterisation to ours.

The data are the monthly factors of the Kenneth French data library, distributed
with this course as a repository snapshot.

Gelfand and Smith (1990). Casella and George (1992). Geweke (1993), Bayesian
treatment of the independent Student-$t$ linear model. Tanner and Wong (1987), on
data augmentation. Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 4. Gelman et al., *Bayesian
Data Analysis* (3rd ed.), ch. 11.
